newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 22.

text.p: THE DOMINION

The Alliance has been pushed further into the cold in coalition talks, with Labour leader Helen Clark indicating on Thursday that it would have no policy input into any Labour-NZ First coalition agreement. Clark said all that was needed from the Alliance was a decision on whether it would support a Labour-led government, if such a deal was put together. She said it would be difficult for Labour and NZ First to amend any coalition agreement to include Alliance policy. Both she and NZ First leader Winston Peters made similar commments on Thursday on the Alliance's role in relation to their two parties, suggesting the two have agreed on a joint position on the Alliance. Page 1.

Treaty Negotiations Minister Doug Graham on Thursday laughed off a NZ First claim that it was Te Tai Tonga MP Tu Wyllie, acting on his own, who initiated a Government about-face at the Privy Council. There was no doubt "at all" that it was NZ First as a party that sparked the action, Graham said. Graham's frank comments made within hours of a statement from NZ First leader Winston Peters that his party had made no approach to Graham about the fisheries assets court hearing, have shattered the careful diplomacy of National toward NZ First as coalition talks continue. Page 1.

In an unusual court move, businessman Selwyn Cushing has been awarded legal costs higher than the $50,000 defamation award they relate to against NZ First leader Winston Peters. The judge awarded on Thursday $75,000 in costs and disbursements. Page 1.

NZ First leader Winston Peters on Thursday appeared to give a suggestion that he could be open to talks on superannuation. His party's policy supporting compulsory superannuation is believed to have been an important sticking point in coalition talks, but it appears Peters may now accept wider discussion of the issue. Page 2.
Police Complaints Authority Sir John Jefferies says he has been "subject to uwanted and improper influence" while investigating the police over the past year. Page 2.

Digruntled Brierley Investments shareholders took their directors to task at the annual meeting in Wellington on Thursday over what one called "the dreadful performance" of the company. BIL reported a tax-paid profit of $310 million for the year to June 30, which was 28 percent down on the previous year. But the group's intrinsic value increased $688 million to $4.19 billion, inclusive of dividend that totalled $241 million. Page 13.

Brierley Investments chairman Bob Matthew hit out on Thursday at critics of the $1 million-plus salaries paid to top executives. BIL was an international company and had to pay international rates to attract top people, he said. Page 13.

Bank of New Zealand returned its third successive record profit on Thursday. BNZ's profit, after tax and minority interests, of $318 million for the year to September 30 was 5.3 percent above 1995's $302 million. Managing director Gordon Wheaton forecast competition in financial services would get tougher yet and put more pressure on margins. Page 13.
Clear Communications has become a full taxpayer in 1996, reflecting a lower net profit of $23 million, but revenue was up 10.83 percent to $266 million for the year ended March 31. Page 13.

New Zealand mining company Summit Gold says early test results are better than expected at its Valhalla uranium deposit in Queensland but it should have a clearer picture in the next few months. Page 14.
International broking house Salomon Brothers is reducing its estimates for Telecom Corporation's net profit in the year ending March 31, 1997 to $775 million from $815 million. Page 14.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

Labour is thinking of beefing up commerce and business-related portfolios into a new Minister of Economic Affairs role and offering it to NZ First leader Winston Peters as an alternative to the finance post. It is understood Labour's coalition negotiators are adamant that Peters does not become Minister of Finance because the financial markets would not accept it.

Telecom is in for more stiff competition -- this time from an internet-based, cut-rate fax service Voyager will launch next month. Fax costs could be slashed by more than half for messages going outside local-calling areas, even for people who have no computer. Voyager's managing director John O'Hara compared his company's proposed 99 cent a minute charge with what he said was Telecom's peak rate of $1.99 a minute for a call between Auckland and London, and 29 cents compared to 75 cents a minute between Auckland and Wellington.

NZ First rejected suggestion on Thursday the party approached the Government over the fisheries assets case about to be heard by the Privy Council. It also rejected a suggestion that one of its MPs Tutekawa Wyllie had a conflict of interest in the matter.

Tne Bank of New Zealand's profit of $318 million for the year to September 30 was a record for any New Zealand bank. It was 5.3 percent up on 1995, despite an intensely competitive environment which had compressed interest margins to 3.3 percent from 3.43 percent, chief executive Gordon Wheaton said.

Though Brierley Investments chairman Bob Matthew was able to cite a 33 percent return to shareholders last year, in a 25 cent share price rise (six cents of it since retraced) and nine cent dividend, shareholders who had invested some years ago in the company remained unimpressed with BIL's performance. One shareholder called for an independent review, by someone like accounting firm Price Waterhouse, of BIL's operations.

Speculation is mounting that Sir Ron Brierley's Guinness Peat Group is building a strategic stake in the brewer DB Group. While the GPG New Zealand director Tony Gibbs declined to comment on Thursday, the market was linking the corporate raider to the recent heavy activity in DB. Since the beginning of the month, the brewer has seen 22 million shares, or nearly six percent of its capital, change hands.

Two minority shareholder critics of Ceramco Corporation have put themselves forward for seats on the board of the troubled company. John Hepburn and Josephine Grierson approached Ceramco directors last month, asking to be considered.
